implementation_notes: Every Python instance stores its attributes in a dictionary, so adding them at runtime, reading them through a runtime string (getattr/setattr) and enumerating them (vars, dir, __dir__) is the language default; __getattr__ supplies computed or missing names when normal lookup fails, and __setattr__ is where validation belongs. types.SimpleNamespace is the minimal owner built for this - the docs note that unlike object, SimpleNamespace allows adding and removing attributes. The classic structure is absorbed; it comes back only when values must be validated or typed, where you hand-write __setattr__ or a data descriptor (property with __set_name__), or delegate to a model library with an explicit extras policy.
pitfalls: On a normal class a typo does not fail: obj.attr = 1 silently creates the attribute, and a read of a missing name raises AttributeError only for classes without __getattr__. Put validation in __setattr__ or use __slots__ when the name set must be closed.

__getattr__ runs only after normal lookup fails while __getattribute__ intercepts everything (and is paid on every access); overriding the wrong one - or recursing through self.attr inside __getattr__ - is the classic bug.

Objects with __slots__ (or a frozen class dictionary) reject dynamic attributes, and dynamic attributes are invisible to static analysis; copies and pickles carry them only if __getstate__/__setstate__ (or __reduce__) include the extra dict.
hasattr() swallows only AttributeError, so a property that raises anything else turns a capability check into a crash.
